title: Integrated Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows
author: Ava Patel
body:
Summary

This controlbook consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance requirements and operational procedures covering: role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) practices, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exceptions. It is intended for engineering, security, and compliance reviewers who implement or verify controls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals and scope
- Ensure least-privilege access for personnel and services across all environments.
- Maintain verifiable immutable audit trails for configuration, authentication, and data access.
- Define clear data residency and retention policies for customer and telemetry data.
- Embed secure SDLC practices from design through release.
- Standardize incident response for security incidents and evidence collection.
- Provide a repeatable compliance evidence workflow for audits and attestations.

Ownership and contact
- Control owner: Security (primary)  Ava Patel (author).
- Supporting teams: eng-infra, eng-sre, eng-serving-runtime, eng-platform, product, legal.
- On-call contact for evidence/requests: security-oncall@redwood.com (pager duty).

1) RBAC & Authentication
Overview
Redwood enforces centralized RBAC for interactive (console/API) and machine identities. All access must be provisioned through standard identity providers (IdP) and service identity systems.

Key principles
- Principle of least privilege: grant only permissions necessary for role-specific tasks.
- Role-based, not user-based, policy attachments for operational services.
- Default deny for any resource not explicitly allowed.
- Short-lived credentials for human and machine access where possible.

Identity providers and federation
- Primary IdP: Okta (OIDC + SAML SSO).
- Service accounts: short-lived tokens via Vault (AWS IAM/STS integration) or Kubernetes serviceAccount + kube2iam.
- For private/on-prem customer deployments, integrate with customer IdP per deployment checklist (see "onprem-packaging" reference).

Role model and common roles (examples)
- security-admin: full security configuration, audit access, exception approvals.
- infra-admin: infra provisioning (no direct access to customer data in hosted default).
- runtime-operator: manage serving runtime, view logs, restart jobs.
- product-reader: view product dashboards, cannot modify infra.
- support-agent: scoped access to customer support tools, requires customer consent for data access.

Provisioning workflow (1-2-3)
1. Request: New role access via Access Request Jira form (access-requests).
2. Approval: Manager + role owner approval required.
3. Provision: Identity team creates group/bindings in IdP and issues temporary credentials.

Policy examples (IAM-like snippet)
- Service role (machine) minimal policy (YAML):

  permissions:
    - action: kms:Decrypt
      resource: arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*
    - action: s3:GetObject
      resource: arn:aws:s3:::redwood-runtime-config/*
    - condition: { 'ForAnyValue:StringEquals': { 'aws:RequestTag/env': 'prod' } }

Human access review
- Quarterly access reviews by role owners.
- Automated reports exported to GRC system (quarterly_review_reports) and stored for 2 years.

2) Audit logging
Overview
All privileged actions, authentication events, administrative API calls, and access to customer data must produce tamper-evident audit logs. Logs must be retained according to data residency policy and made available for incident response and compliance audits.

Log sources and retention
- Auth logs: IdP (Okta)  retained 365 days by default for identities associated with hosted accounts.
- Infrastructure logs: CloudTrail (AWS), GCP Audit Logs  retained 365 days for funded customer tiers; shorter for dev environments (90 days).
- Application-access logs: Redwood API gateway (per-request metadata, auth subject, model, route)  retained 365 days for enterprise customers and 90 days for standard.
- Audit-trail integrity: logs are written to immutable S3 buckets with WORM enabled and checksummed daily.

Log format and fields (table described)
- Each audit entry must include: timestamp (UTC), request_id, principal_id, principal_type (user/service), action, resource, outcome (success/failure), ip_address, region, trace_id.

Example log line (JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-10T14:22:03Z",
  "request_id": "req-0a1b2c3d",
  "principal_id": "user:alice@redwood.com",
  "principal_type": "user",
  "action": "admin:grant-role",
  "resource": "group:runtime-operators",
  "outcome": "success",
  "ip_address": "203.0.113.42",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "trace_id": "trace-7f8e9d"
}

Alerting and SLOs for logging
- Audit log pipeline availability SLO: 99.9% ingestion over 30d.
- Alert: if any log stream lag exceeds 10 minutes for >5 minutes, paging to eng-sre.
- Integrity check: daily checksum job must run; failures escalate to security-oncall immediately.

Access to logs
- Access to raw logs requires security-admin or explicit approval.
- Aggregated dashboards and search access are provisioned via read-only roles.

3) Data residency & retention
Policy principles
- Customer data must be stored in customer-approved regions. Default hosted regions: us-west-2, eu-west-1, asia-southeast-1 (partners).
- Telemetry and telemetry-derived data must be pseudonymized before cross-region transfer.
- Retention windows are defined by data classification and customer contract.

Classification & retention matrix (summary)
- Customer PII: retention = contract-based, default: 2 years (negotiable).
- Customer non-PII (models inputs/outputs): default retention 90 days for standard, 365 days for enterprise unless customer sets their own retention.
- Platform telemetry (metrics/heartbeat): 13 months for aggregated metrics, 90 days for raw traces.
- Audit logs: 365 days standard, WORM buckets for enterprise longer retention options.

Residency enforcement checklist
1. Deployment region pinning in customer manifest (required).
2. S3/GCS buckets tagged with residency label and policy enforced via org SCPs/IAM conditions.
3. Cross-region replication disabled unless explicitly authorized.
4. Customer data-at-rest encryption using customer-managed KMS keys when required.

Retention & deletion workflow
- Automated retention job runs daily; entities marked for deletion are moved to a "quarantine" bucket for 30 days (for recovery/forensics) before permanent deletion.
- Deletion must produce an audit event with deletion rationale and owner.

4) Secure SDLC (secure development lifecycle)
Overview
Secure SDLC at Redwood integrates threat modeling, code review, dependency scanning, secrets management, static and dynamic analysis, and gated deployment.

Required controls
- Threat modeling: required for all major features and changes that handle customer data; stored as a Confluence artifact and reviewed by Security.
- Pull request rules: minimum 2 approvers for production-impacting changes, one must be from a different team.
- Automated scanning: SCA (software composition analysis) and SAST on all PRs; failed critical findings block merge.
- Secrets: no secrets in code; secrets stored in Vault with RBAC. Scans run nightly to detect leaks.
- CI/CD gating: builds must pass unit tests, security checks, and signed artifacts before release.

Release controls and rollback
- Canary rollout for runtime changes: 5% traffic for 30 minutes, automated health checks.
- Automated rollback if latency or error budget exceeds thresholds (see performance-standards).
- Post-release security smoke tests for abnormal auth/access patterns executed within 1 hour.

Developer checklist (short)
- Add threat model and test plan to PR description.
- Ensure SCA & SAST pass or documented risk.
- Specify rollout policy in release manifest.

5) Incident response security procedures
Incident classes and priorities
- Priority 1 (P1): confirmed data exfiltration or compromise of production keys  immediate page to security-oncall and execs.
- Priority 2 (P2): suspected unauthorized access to customer data or critical infra degradation.
- Priority 3 (P3): non-critical vulnerabilities with credible exploit but no evidence of active compromise.

Initial triage steps (numbered playbook)
1. Identification: Capture scope, affected services, and indicators of compromise. Create incident in the incident system with a unique incident ID.
2. Containment: Apply short-term mitigations (rotate keys, block IPs, remove compromised host from LB).
3. Evidence collection: Preserve logs, snapshots, metadata (see evidence collection checklist below).
4. Eradication: Remove malicious artifacts, patch vulnerabilities.
5. Recovery: Restore services with hardened configs; monitor for reappearance for 72 hours.
6. Lessons learned: Postmortem within 7 business days, assign action items and owners.

Evidence collection checklist
- Snapshot of relevant hosts (AMIs/EBS snapshots) with tags: incident_id, owner, timestamp.
- Extracted immutable audit logs for the relevant timeframe and principal.
- Network captures (pcap) if applicable; store in WORM bucket.
- Hashes (SHA256) of artifacts and copies, and chain-of-custody notes.
- List of rotated credentials and time of rotation.

Privacy & customer notification
- For incidents involving customer data, follow the customer-notification policy and legal must be engaged within 24 hours of confirmation.
- Notification windows and templates are in the customer-incident-communications page.

6) Compliance evidence workflows
Purpose
Provide a repeatable process to collect, store, and present artifacts for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, customer-specific assessments).

Evidence types and storage
- Policies & procedures (Confluence)  canonical page + PDF snapshot exported quarterly.
- Logs and telemetry  immutable WORM buckets; access controlled and audited.
- Configuration snapshots  infrastructure-as-code repo tags and deployment manifests.
- Interview notes and attestations  recorded in the GRC system with approver signatures.

Standard evidence request process
1. Request submission: Auditor or internal stakeholder creates a request in GRC ticketing.
2. Triage and owner assignment: Security assigns evidence owner within 2 business days.
3. Collection: Owner collects artifacts, documents collection steps, and uploads to evidence repo.
4. Review: Security reviews artifacts and marks as "compliant" or notes exceptions.
5. Delivery: Evidence delivered via secure share (SFTP/secure portal) with audit of access.

Retention of evidence
- Evidence for completed audits retained 7 years unless contractually specified otherwise.

7) Risk and exceptions
Risk management approach
- All deviations from control requirements must be treated as risks and entered into the risk register with compensating controls, owner, and expiry.

Exception request template (fields)
- request_id, owner, control_affected, justification, compensating_controls, expiration_date, approval_status, approvers.

Exception approval process
1. Submit exception via the Exceptions Jira form with detailed justification and risk assessment.
2. Security reviews and proposes compensating controls; may escalate to CISO for high-risk exceptions.
3. Exception approved with a maximum duration of 90 days (unless executive  up to 1 year), with mandatory quarterly review.

Compensating controls examples
- Increased monitoring and alerting for the affected resource.
- Network isolation and IP allowlist.
- Additional manual approval gates in deployment pipelines.

Periodic reviews and metrics
- Quarterly compliance scorecard published to execs with: outstanding exceptions, exception age distribution, audit findings open >30 days, and average remediation time.
- KPIs: mean time to evidence collection (target < 3 business days), percentage of access reviews completed (target 100% quarterly), number of high-risk exceptions (target 0).

Appendices
A. Useful CLI snippets and checks
- Verify active IAM sessions (example AWS CLI):
  aws sts get-session-token --duration-seconds 3600

- Export recent audit logs (example S3 copy):
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-audit-logs/2026/08/10/ /local/logs/ --recursive --profile audit-reader

B. Evidence collection command examples
- Take EBS snapshot with tags (example):
  aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "incident-1234-2026-08-10" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=snapshot,Tags=[{Key=incident_id,Value=INC-1234},{Key=owner,Value=security}]'

C. References and related pages

Notes
- This document is a control-level summary and links to implementation runbooks and playbooks for operational detail. For any deployment or audit-specific deviations, follow the exception workflow above and notify the security team.
